nodes.label: BFS: a filesystem shaped like a database
nodes.norm_label: bfs: a filesystem shaped like a database
nodes.rationale: BeOS used an actual relational database as its filesystem through DR8 and pulled it: too complex to maintain, too costly in performance. At DR9 they rewrote it as a directory hierarchy with attributes and an indexed attribute pool, lost very little and gained a lot of speed. The most useful warning in the book.

nodes.label: Entity files (BeOS People files)
nodes.rationale: Files with no content - just a name and attributes. Drag one into a mail client and it knows you want to send mail; into a fax program and it goes out over the fax number. It fits Kosmos because a namespace node already returns a table.

nodes.label: The three always-indexed attributes
nodes.rationale: BFS indexed name, size and modification date on every file, always, which is why a query by name was a targeted index lookup rather than a walk. Decision: those three are always indexed without anyone asking; other attributes get indexed when declared.

nodes.label: Attributes
nodes.rationale: Typed metadata alongside a file, indexed by the filesystem. What makes live queries possible.

nodes.label: Live query
nodes.rationale: Registering a predicate over attributes and receiving a message when the result set changes. No polling. It is the BeOS feature nobody replicated.

nodes.label: Get Info, and editing attributes from the desktop
nodes.norm_label: get info, and editing attributes from the desktop

nodes.label: A filesystem of its own, with a journal
nodes.norm_label: a filesystem of its own, with a journal
nodes.rationale: Checked against power loss by killing the machine at an exact instant rather than hoping. Attributes on files, and live queries over them.

nodes.label: A name in the query index
nodes.norm_label: a name in the query index

nodes.label: console server
nodes.rationale: The interesting conversion: it is the one protocol with two implementations, since a terminal window mounts itself as its child's /dev/console and the runner that mounts it cannot tell which it got - the capability discipline working correctly. So the layout is compiled once into a kit and both sides go through it. read also stopped blocking inside a handler; the C server records who asked and answers from the loop.

nodes.label: /kits/gl
nodes.rationale: A GL context costs ten bytes a pixel out of a two-megabyte heap. TinyGL asserts rather than returning when an allocation fails, and an assert here is a panic, so the kit refuses a context it cannot afford and says what would fit. The budget is three quarters of the heap, measured rather than chosen: half was tried first and would have refused a size that demonstrably worked, which is the more annoying way to be wrong about a limit because it looks like caution.

nodes.label: httpd
nodes.rationale: nginx's shape - one process, an event loop, and a coroutine per connection - because there is no thread syscall at all: SYS_SPAWN makes a process, and a process has one lua_State, so two threads inside one would want a lock around the interpreter and would take turns anyway. The coroutine is why serve still reads as a straight line, with a yield wherever it used to wait.

nodes.label: Terminal
nodes.rationale: It is a console server - it speaks the same write and read that /dev/console speaks and hands itself to its children under that name - which is the design working rather than a trick played on it. No program knows or can ask what is behind /dev/console. A window that is somebody's console cannot poll once a second, so ui has a poll_wait the Terminal sets to one tick.

nodes.label: tests/tests.c
nodes.rationale: 127 checks, 4,085 lines, the largest single test asset in the tree - and it has never run on x86-64, because there is no x86 test image target for TEST=1 to build. The suite that most directly exercises the kernel has run on one board only. Left open by the 0.9 review as real work rather than a line.

nodes.label: webserver app
nodes.rationale: The manager is not the server and that is forced: accept blocks and a window that blocked would stop drawing. They talk through /data - the server writes its state and last forty lines, the manager reads them on a tick - which is a file rather than a message because the server has no idea anybody is watching.

nodes.label: Doubled lists that nothing checks agree
nodes.norm_label: doubled lists that nothing checks agree
nodes.rationale: X86_FLAGS against CFLAGS_BASE lost three things in a row, each found only when something broke - the user base address, the screen size, and the heap size. The last killed the TinyGL demos with a page fault at USER_HEAP plus exactly 512 pages, because the kernel mapped 512 and the userland compiled into it believed 3072.

nodes.label: Slice-based edits silently delete code
nodes.rationale: Three times: nine test functions, then tests_run() and bench_run() - which read as make test hanging rather than failing - then run_program, which killed the shell silently because the shell prints by asking the console server. The rule is narrow anchors.

nodes.label: IPI - inter-processor interrupt
nodes.rationale: Needed for cross-core IPC and for TLB shootdown.

nodes.label: Memory barrier
nodes.rationale: dsb, dmb, isb. Necessary because AArch64 has a weak memory model.

nodes.label: TLB shootdown
nodes.rationale: On AArch64 the broadcast is done in hardware (TLBI with an IS suffix), which saves considerable work compared to x86.

nodes.label: Weak memory model
nodes.rationale: x86 has TSO, which is far more conservative. Code that works on x86 can fail on ARM without barriers, once every thousand boots.

nodes.label: The seven-step order
nodes.rationale: Per-CPU struct with NR_CPUS = 1; locks taken uncontended on one core; a second core parked; the idle thread on it; per-CPU runqueues; IPIs; TLB shootdown. The kernel is correct at every step and make test still passes, which is what makes it safe incrementally.

nodes.label: IPIs for preempting a remote core
nodes.norm_label: ipis for preempting a remote core

nodes.norm_label: per-cpu runqueues behind the scheduler vtable

nodes.label: TLB shootdown as the last step
nodes.norm_label: tlb shootdown as the last step

nodes.label: Do SMP on AArch64 first
nodes.rationale: x86-64 is total-store-ordered and forgives reorderings AArch64 does not. A locking discipline correct on ARM is correct on x86; one developed on x86 will be wrong on ARM in ways that appear once every few thousand boots, the most expensive class of bug this project has.

nodes.label: gfxbench
nodes.rationale: Measures the primitives under QEMU: fill 214 Mpx/s, blit 48, span 80. The number is QEMU's; the ratio between the rows is what transfers.

nodes.label: The drawing model: commands, not a shared buffer
nodes.norm_label: the drawing model: commands, not a shared buffer
nodes.rationale: Model B, the X11 and BeOS app_server model: pure message passing, no new kernel primitive, and commands are data that can be logged, replayed, redirected or inspected. Shared memory is added as a special case, never the general one.

nodes.label: Doom, the ideal shape
nodes.rationale: It renders a frame inside its own C loop and hands over one buffer: one crossing per frame rather than one per shape. The headroom is not the interesting part - the shape is.

nodes.label: The shared-memory pixel path
nodes.rationale: Commands cover 95% of what the system draws; this is the other 5% - apps that produce pixels, where commands are no use and you drop down to shared memory. A different path that has to be designed separately.

nodes.label: The direct window (direct = true)
nodes.rationale: Requested explicitly and justified: for a surface that changes wholesale, and for typography, since the compositor rasterises in the four faces the desktop chose. The trade is absolute - a direct window has no widgets, so its chrome is rectangles the application knows the position of. It buys the page and charges for the toolbar.

nodes.label: Draw produces a list of commands
nodes.norm_label: draw produces a list of commands
nodes.rationale: gc accumulates tables and sends them in one message. Commands being data allows caching a view's list, logging and replaying drawing, inspecting from the REPL, and redirecting to another display without the app knowing.

nodes.label: No GPU: the framebuffer is enough
nodes.norm_label: no gpu: the framebuffer is enough
nodes.rationale: 1920x1080 at 32bpp is 8.3 MB a frame, 500 MB/s at 60fps, against ~17 GB/s of real bandwidth - an order of magnitude spare, and with damage tracking the whole screen is never redrawn.

nodes.label: What a Lua/C crossing costs
nodes.rationale: About 9 microseconds, which buys about two thousand pixels - so a 30-pixel span is 99% overhead and a 32x32 tile is break-even. A primitive should write about two thousand pixels or be called in a batch. The same disc is 3 Mpx/s span-per-row from Lua and 103 Mpx/s as one call.

nodes.label: audioring.h - SPSC period ring
nodes.rationale: Replaced a 1024-byte period travelling as a message payload 172 times a second, which manufactured 340 KB/s of garbage inside a 5.8 ms deadline. It happened because MSG_BYTES is 2048 and a period is 1024 - it fit, and fitting is the trap.

nodes.label: ramfs (/data)
nodes.rationale: Converted to C so the system would be one thing rather than six servers in C and one in Lua for a feature's sake, at a price known in advance. Conversion found that /data had always stored Lua values rather than bytes, so the namespace packs and the server holds bytes with a flag. It also kept its store in .bss - static struct node nodes[128], 2.1 MB - so every process carried a copy of a server's private storage; it asks for the pages at startup now.

nodes.label: tcpring.h - two SPSC rings in a shared region
nodes.norm_label: tcpring.h - two spsc rings in a shared region
nodes.rationale: Written down before a byte moved rather than after somebody found a message worked for the first ten kilobytes. The receive window is the ring's free space, not a number the stack invented - a window is a promise, and a client that stops reading really does slow the sender down.

nodes.label: Hot reload (removed)
nodes.rationale: It was real - M5 proved it with a server's code replaced mid-conversation - and it worked because state and behaviour are separate: serve takes a factory, so anything in state survives and anything captured in a closure is lost. Then the disagreement stopped happening because the servers ran out; ramfs was the last one that could be reloaded, and converting it deleted ROLE_RELOAD. Do not describe it as a tiebreaker any more. What survives is the shape, and level 2 where a supervisor restarts a server that died.

nodes.label: Read-only image mapped rather than copied
nodes.norm_label: read-only image mapped rather than copied
nodes.rationale: Code, fonts, icons and the Lua source of every program - 2.8 MB - are one set of physical pages for the machine, read-only and executable at EL0. Permissions live in the mapping rather than in the page, so nothing about isolation changes. A process holds 2224 KB where it held 7232; a whole desktop with a 3D cube holds 47 MB where it held 148. The test had to be rewritten: 'separate address spaces' checked that two processes' code was a different physical page, which was a proxy for isolation and is now deliberately false.

nodes.label: Control by message, data by shared memory
nodes.norm_label: control by message, data by shared memory
nodes.rationale: A message says what to do; a region holds what to do it to. The test is the rate: if it recurs because the hardware says so - a frame, a period, a packet, a block - the bytes live in a region and the message carries only where and how much. Learned expensively from the audio server. The discipline that comes with it is single-producer single-consumer rings with indices.

nodes.label: Single-producer single-consumer ring
nodes.rationale: One side only writes, one side only reads, nobody takes a lock, and the indices are the only thing both touch. Anything that wants more than that wants a message.

nodes.label: Doom
nodes.rationale: Seven bugs on the way and the two the system owned are the ones to remember: snprintf ignored precision on integers, so %.3d of 33 gave 33 and the HUD font lumps came out one character short - a missing-file error caused by a formatting bug; and C output from a windowed process vanished entirely because SYS_WRITE is refused unless the process owns the console, so forty thousand lines started up, failed and said nothing.

nodes.label: Binned, growing malloc
nodes.rationale: malloc was a first-fit scan over one list holding every block, free or allocated, so an allocation cost what the heap already contained. Free blocks are binned by size class with the bin links inside each free block's own payload, which costs nothing because the minimum payload is exactly two pointers. alloc_table 79x faster; serialize fell 40% untouched. The heap also grows by asking the kernel for another arena, which retires the DOOM=1 heap flag. The trap written into the code: sys_map never reuses an address, so arenas are not adjacent and each must be its own physical list with NULL at both ends.

nodes.label: /kits/web
nodes.rationale: The whole libc bill for a hundred and forty thousand lines of HTML parser, CSS engine and DOM came to three functions: bsearch, strtoul and time. That was the question Tier 0 existed to answer - whether this libc holds up under serious third-party C.

nodes.label: Context switch
nodes.rationale: Written in assembly, and getting it wrong corrupts things that only show up five functions later.

nodes.label: ESR / ELR / FAR
nodes.rationale: The three together turn a hang into a useful message: what kind of exception, which instruction, and what address.

nodes.label: One kernel check failed once
nodes.rationale: 1 of 127, and not since. The evidence was destroyed by a grep that kept only the summary line. Recorded as intermittent rather than fixed, because nothing fixed it.

nodes.label: The exception handler that prints ESR, ELR and FAR
nodes.norm_label: the exception handler that prints esr, elr and far
nodes.rationale: The best investment in the project: it turns a silent hang into a message telling you which instruction faulted and on what address.

nodes.label: GDB against QEMU
nodes.rationale: Earns its keep on context switch bugs, which are nearly impossible to find with prints.

nodes.label: What to do when you get stuck
nodes.norm_label: what to do when you get stuck
nodes.rationale: Instrument over UART to the last line that executed; check barriers and cache maintenance; verify MMIO against the datasheet rather than memory; compare with QEMU if the bug is on hardware or the other way; reduce to the smallest reproduction.

nodes.label: Debugging without a debugger, over the UART
nodes.norm_label: debugging without a debugger, over the uart
nodes.rationale: A putchar that works from the third instruction is the first thing to build. When something hangs, instrument until you find the last line that executed - bisecting with puts is primitive and it is the fastest thing there is. On real hardware there is no GDB, only UART.

nodes.label: Deskbar
nodes.rationale: It asks the window manager what is on screen rather than asking /app what registered, because a program that opens a window directly has one and no registration. Four sections - Applications, System, Preferences, Demos - because a preference is a choice that stays chosen, and the network configuration, process list, log and web server are windows onto services running right now.

nodes.label: /bin reported 74 of its 82 programs
nodes.rationale: A listing reply holds BIN_CHUNK / BIN_NAME_MAX = 74 names and BIN_OP_LIST started at nought every time. The eight dropped were the last alphabetically and four were applications, so the Deskbar could not offer Tracker, the Terminal, the top bar or the web server. Nothing failed; the menu was just short. The guard was a _Static_assert that cannot check the number of programs, so it watched the chunk shrinking while the image grew past it.

nodes.label: Scripting architecture (/app)
nodes.rationale: An application answers for its own properties because it called ui.window, not because it has any scripting code. The registry hands out capabilities and never forwards, so one slow application cannot hold everyone else's door.

nodes.label: Declared shape (struct protocols)
nodes.rationale: A server receives exactly what it expects, not whatever somebody put in a table: a fixed-field struct means most wrong shapes cannot be expressed, so the wire refuses them and the server never has to check. audioproto.h, devproto.h, binproto.h, appproto.h and conproto.h are the headers both sides compile against. The cost is real - editing a header and rebuilding both sides, and errors are numbers - and it moved the collector out of the server and into every client on the frame path until con.wait did the exchange in C.

nodes.label: Big-endian / little-endian
nodes.rationale: PowerPC is big-endian; ARM and x86 are little-endian. Mixing them forces you to define an explicit wire format.

nodes.label: Open Firmware
nodes.rationale: The firmware on PowerPC Macs: a Forth environment that stays alive after loading your kernel and exposes a console and a device tree.

nodes.label: PowerPC, on a G5 or a G4 iMac
nodes.norm_label: powerpc, on a g5 or a g4 imac
nodes.rationale: It changes two things written down as settled: it is big-endian, and the G4 is 32-bit against a principle that says Kosmos is 64-bit only. The rule for a principle in the way is to say which one, say what it costs, and decide deliberately rather than drift.

nodes.label: The big-endian audit
nodes.rationale: Done before there was any reason to need it and it holds: every string.pack in the on-disk format carries an explicit <, a tree-wide search for native-endian packs finds none, and the network stack builds big-endian by construction with byte shifts. What would move is runtime/include/endian.h, which becomes per-architecture.

nodes.label: No POSIX personality at system level
nodes.norm_label: no posix personality at system level
nodes.rationale: A libc inside an app is fine and necessary; fork, signals, global descriptors and a tree reachable without a namespace are forbidden. It means ports get patched rather than accommodated, and that is the deliberate price of the rest.

nodes.label: BeOS was POSIX-compatible; Kosmos is not
nodes.norm_label: beos was posix-compatible; kosmos is not
nodes.rationale: BeOS could afford POSIX because its resource model was the same old global tree; Kosmos has per-process namespaces and capabilities, and a POSIX personality would destroy both. The cost is real - BeOS had an ecosystem of ported software and Kosmos will have none - and is accepted in exchange for the result of the experiment.

nodes.label: What it is not: Unix, Windows, macOS, AmigaOS, a BeOS clone
nodes.norm_label: what it is not: unix, windows, macos, amigaos, a beos clone
nodes.rationale: No fork, exec, signals, pipes, sockets, select, ioctl, file descriptors, or a path reachable without a namespace. AmigaOS's lack of memory protection is the thing this is furthest from. And not a BeOS clone though BeOS is the reference: BeOS was monolithic, and the architecture underneath here is QNX's.

nodes.label: longjmp
nodes.rationale: Lua uses it for error handling, and it is the reason Rust does not fit well as the kernel language here: destructors never run.

nodes.label: setjmp/longjmp demands the most care
nodes.rationale: Lua uses it for error handling, and getting it wrong produces a bug that only shows up when something raises an error, long afterwards.

nodes.label: Never edit lua/upstream directly
nodes.rationale: Freestanding changes live in lua/patches and are applied during the build, so a new upstream version updates without fighting your own changes. Ten minutes now, a week later.

nodes.label: Typed attributes and live queries
nodes.rationale: Attributes live alongside the file, typed and indexed. A predicate registered over them makes the server push when the result set changes - the BeOS part nobody replicated.

nodes.label: Capabilities by index into a per-process array
nodes.norm_label: capabilities by index into a per-process array
nodes.rationale: A process cannot name what it was not handed: no global table to enumerate, no path to guess. Simpler than Unix permissions and better isolation.

nodes.label: The criticality hierarchy
nodes.rationale: As in Erlang: complexity goes far from the root. The namespace is not restartable and is kept boring; framebuffer and input are restartable but visible; everything else is restartable.

nodes.label: One real filesystem on disk
nodes.rationale: Same file for two processes, no copies and no divergent views; what does not exist is every app seeing the whole tree. It is what a container does on Linux, except here it is the only form there is.

nodes.label: The inspector, the first app
nodes.rationale: A window listing processes and namespaces with a REPL against any live server - the tool used for the rest of development and the proof that the design closes.

nodes.label: Synchronous rendezvous IPC
nodes.rationale: L4 style, no kernel buffering: simpler, faster on the hot path, and it avoids the queue-and-backpressure hell that ate Mach. Destroying an endpoint must wake everyone blocked on it with an error.

nodes.label: The kernel at EL1, fixed pools, no allocator
nodes.norm_label: the kernel at el1, fixed pools, no allocator
nodes.rationale: Everything in statically declared fixed-size pools eliminates half the possible memory bugs in one stroke. It knows nothing about files, networking, graphics or Lua.

nodes.label: A large read returns a memory capability
nodes.norm_label: a large read returns a memory capability
nodes.rationale: A 936 KB PNG through fs.read gives 'not enough memory' on a 2 MB heap, so the server puts the pages in a region and the capability travels in the reply. A message is 2048 bytes, and the answer to moving a megabyte is never 'in smaller messages'.

nodes.label: The in-process libc
nodes.rationale: Every libc I/O function is a call into the process's namespace and nothing else, with no fallback to a global tree. Never fork, exec, signal, pipe, socket, select, ioctl or unistd.h; errno is per process.

nodes.label: The app manifest and its declared needs
nodes.norm_label: the app manifest and its declared needs
nodes.rationale: The launcher builds the namespace with exactly what is declared, so the app reaches nothing else because nothing else exists in its world. Even the clock is a capability.

nodes.label: Monitor, the example app
nodes.rationale: Everything it reads comes from servers exposing a namespace: /proc is not a special filesystem, it is a server answering list and read in the same protocol as the SD card.

nodes.label: Per-process namespace
nodes.rationale: What a process has not mounted does not exist - not permission denied, no such path. Clients hold a namespace node rather than a permanent capability, which is what lets a server die and come back.

nodes.label: Notes, the example app
nodes.rationale: A real filesystem plus attributes and live queries: fs.query registers a predicate and the server notifies when the result set changes.

nodes.label: One userland image, a process is that binary with a different argument
nodes.norm_label: one userland image, a process is that binary with a different argument
nodes.rationale: No loader, no ELF parser, no relocation. It is what makes bootstrap possible at all: init spawns binfs, and binfs cannot be loaded from binfs.

nodes.label: Kosmos packages, resolved against the namespace
nodes.norm_label: kosmos packages, resolved against the namespace
nodes.rationale: require resolves against the process's namespace, not a global path, so two processes can see different versions of a library without conflict.

nodes.label: One protocol for every resource
nodes.rationale: Typed records rather than byte streams: list, read, write, getattr, setattr, query. read returns a table, which is where BeOS typed attributes go inside the Plan 9 primitive.

nodes.label: Read-only image pages mapped, not copied
nodes.norm_label: read-only image pages mapped, not copied
nodes.rationale: 2.8 MB of .text/.rodata mapped read-only at USER_TEXT_VA in every address space; only the 112 KB writable half is copied. Permissions live in the mapping, not the page, and both mappings share attributes, so the alias is safe. Took a process from 7232 KB to 2224 KB.

nodes.label: Level 2: a supervisor restarts a dead server
nodes.norm_label: level 2: a supervisor restarts a dead server
nodes.rationale: Clients reconnect through the namespace. It never depended on the language a server was written in, and it is the architectural property.

nodes.label: The font server that is not built yet
nodes.norm_label: the font server that is not built yet
nodes.rationale: The weak argument is duplication, which shared read-only image pages fix instead. The real argument is the parser: an untrusted file parsed in fourteen address spaces becomes one process that can die and be restarted. Glyph-per-IPC is not allowed at 9us a crossing, so the server owns the faces and hands out an atlas per (face, size) as a shared region.

nodes.label: Outline fonts, and why there are three faces
nodes.norm_label: outline fonts, and why there are three faces
nodes.rationale: The bitmap font stays the default because it is exact and costs nothing. ui, text and mono want different things and the terminal's must be fixed-width, which is not a preference. Five faces took the user image from 577 KB to 1433 KB, and every process gets a private copy - about 19.6 MB spent on the same bytes fourteen times, which is a property of the image rather than of fonts.

nodes.label: Who frees a shared surface's pages
nodes.norm_label: who frees a shared surface's pages
nodes.rationale: A region is refcounted and its pages go back when the last capability drops, not when a process that mapped it exits. The rule is an address range rather than a flag on a page: shared regions map at USER_SHARE_VA, a window nothing frees by walking. Both bump pointers need a ceiling, and shared pages are charged once, to whoever created the region.

nodes.label: stb_truetype
nodes.rationale: Vendored unmodified, handling TrueType and CFF. Its own header says it offers no security guarantee against untrusted font files; what contains it today is where it runs - EL0, in whichever process is drawing - and that stops being sufficient the moment fonts arrive from somewhere other than the build.

nodes.label: Replicants
nodes.rationale: A view is Lua source plus a state table, both serialisable, and a replicant is a message carrying source, state and needs; the host loads it and mounts exactly what needs declares. The honest limit: it runs inside its host's process, so the restriction is the language's rather than the kernel's - more than BeOS offered, less than a separate process. Evidence has to come from inside the replicant, not from the host.

nodes.label: The index is rebuilt at mount, never stored
nodes.norm_label: the index is rebuilt at mount, never stored
nodes.rationale: Derivable state that is also stored is state that can disagree with itself, which on a filesystem means a query returning a file that is not there. It holds while a mount scan is cheaper than the complexity it avoids.

nodes.label: The POSIX line
nodes.rationale: POSIX is four assumptions - a global tree, ambient authority, fork and signals - and all four collide with the design. A layer that works becomes a second OS sharing the kernel, and it has gravity: it is what happened to Haiku.

nodes.label: Isolation from the hardware, not from the language
nodes.norm_label: isolation from the hardware, not from the language
nodes.rationale: Lua is not isolated by default and does not need to be: isolation is the EL0 address space plus capability validation. Loading precompiled bytecode is forbidden and the library list is part of the security model.

nodes.label: Who owns the state when a server dies
nodes.norm_label: who owns the state when a server dies
nodes.rationale: Three ways out in order of effort: state reconstructible from the client (enough for Kosmos), state in a separate store server (the good version), and persistent state (the rejected single-level store).

nodes.label: What stays out, and the achievable goal
nodes.norm_label: what stays out, and the achievable goal
nodes.rationale: A daily driver needs a browser, and that is where projects die maintaining somebody else's port. The criterion for every decision: does this test an idea in the design, or close a feature gap against Linux?

nodes.label: BMessages
nodes.rationale: Drag a colour onto the desktop and it changes colour; drag the same colour into a text editor and it inserts the hex value. Neither app was programmed to talk to the colour picker. In Kosmos these are Lua tables with a type field, and they are the same thing that travels between servers.

nodes.label: BLooper / BHandler / BMessage
nodes.rationale: A BLooper was a thread with a message queue; a BMessage a typed dictionary. In Kosmos they are coroutines and Lua tables.

nodes.label: BView
nodes.rationale: A rectangle that knows how to draw itself and receive events, with coordinates relative to its parent. The Kosmos equivalent is the UI kit's view.

nodes.label: Follow modes
nodes.rationale: Each view declares which edges of the parent it stays attached to. Fifty lines, against the thousands of a constraint solver.

nodes.label: Tooling: test, screenshot, bench, stress, release
nodes.norm_label: tooling: test, screenshot, bench, stress, release

nodes.label: make stress becomes the SMP test
nodes.norm_label: make stress becomes the smp test
nodes.rationale: It already asks the right question - use the machine hard, then ask sysinfo whether it gave everything back - because a lost lock shows up as a leaked slot. What it cannot do is find an ordering bug, and nothing can reliably.

nodes.label: The MediaOS focus - not copied
nodes.rationale: BeOS's whole design was oriented toward real-time video and audio. Kosmos does not have that goal, and the decisions BeOS made for it enter only where they earn their place for another reason.

nodes.label: The Translation Kit - not copied
nodes.rationale: A central library of translators where a new one extended many apps at once. Good idea, out of scope.

nodes.label: EL0 / EL1 / EL2 / EL3
nodes.rationale: Which level you are handed depends on the machine and its options, so read CurrentEL rather than assuming.

nodes.label: File types as a preferences application
nodes.norm_label: file types as a preferences application
nodes.rationale: Rather than a table compiled into the image.

nodes.label: SSH, in layers with test vectors
nodes.norm_label: ssh, in layers with test vectors
nodes.rationale: The binary packet protocol, Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, userauth, channels. The one place here where a bug is silent - a wrong nonce keeps working and is not secure - so 'it connected' is not evidence.

nodes.label: TLS
nodes.rationale: Without it most of the web refuses to speak.

nodes.label: Statically declared kernel pools
nodes.rationale: 48 threads, 32 processes, 96 endpoints, 32 address spaces. Running out is an error at a known limit rather than a failure at an unknown one, and every number is reported by ps because a limit nothing counts is a limit nobody can find.

nodes.label: Pervasive multithreading - pushing sand, not rocks
nodes.norm_label: pervasive multithreading - pushing sand, not rocks
nodes.rationale: Nobody computes faster, but everything responds better because everything gets constant attention in small pieces. Creating a BeOS window spawned two threads. Kosmos keeps the property - a busy window does not freeze the others - and changes the mechanism to coroutines.

nodes.label: Coroutine
nodes.rationale: Concurrency without parallelism and without locks. It is what makes it possible to write sequential code over synchronous IPC.

nodes.label: Kosmos (the operating system)
nodes.rationale: Nebula plus the servers, the namespace, the desktop and the applications. What somebody uses. The two names are not interchangeable.

nodes.label: Microkernel
nodes.rationale: The kernel does the minimum - threads, memory, IPC - and everything else runs in userland processes. The opposite is monolithic.

nodes.label: Nebula (the microkernel)
nodes.rationale: Threads, address spaces, IPC, capabilities and nothing else. What kernel/, arch/ and hal/ build into. It does not know what a file, a pixel or a network is.

nodes.label: Synchronous IPC / rendezvous
nodes.rationale: The sender blocks until the receiver is ready, with no buffering in the kernel. Simpler and faster than asynchronous, at the cost of code being harder to write - and coroutines solve that.

nodes.label: A microkernel, from QNX
nodes.source_location: And the rest of what it is built out of

nodes.label: Versions are major.minor.revision
nodes.rationale: A revision per push, a minor when something substantial lands. There is no release schedule and nothing is stable - the version number is a bookmark, not a promise.

nodes.label: A non-blocking send
nodes.rationale: Half a browser frame is the application blocked on a commit whose handler swaps an index and records a rectangle. SYS_CALL, SYS_RECEIVE and SYS_REPLY are the whole IPC surface and every message blocks for its reply by construction, so triple buffering cannot fix it. It is a change to the IPC model: a syscall, a fixed-size queue in the endpoint struct, a decision about what a full queue does, and backpressure.

nodes.label: The pools are the easy locks
nodes.norm_label: the pools are the easy locks
nodes.rationale: threads[], processes[], endpoints[], objects[] and the physical bitmap are arrays with an allocation function each. One lock apiece around allocate and free is correct and uncontended.

nodes.label: SMP - what it would take
nodes.rationale: Nothing here is written yet. Counted against the code as it stands rather than estimated, because the last thing written down about SMP was wrong for two years.

nodes.label: The kernel as the narrowest box
nodes.norm_label: the kernel as the narrowest box
nodes.rationale: The textbook Unix diagram makes the kernel the widest box because a filesystem, a terminal and drawing are all kernel code. Kosmos inverts it: almost everything that picture puts inside the kernel is a process beside the shell rather than underneath it.

nodes.label: The stale SMP-ready claim
nodes.rationale: This document still says the code is written SMP-ready with a per-CPU runqueue and TPIDR_EL1. docs/smp.md counts the same claim and finds none of the three has ever existed.

nodes.label: Threads with shared memory, and the locking API it cost
nodes.norm_label: threads with shared memory, and the locking api it cost
nodes.rationale: BeOS pushed threads and shared memory into userland and paid with Lock() and Unlock() on every window and an entire class of bugs. Kosmos uses coroutines and share-nothing, and that class of bug does not exist.

nodes.label: There are no milestones any more
nodes.norm_label: there are no milestones any more
nodes.rationale: Thirteen numbered milestones were the right shape for a kernel that did not boot yet, and the numbers went on being quoted long after they described anything: the README said M6, graphics while the machine had a journalled filesystem, a TCP/IP stack and a web browser. A number that no longer means anything is worse than no number, because it is read as though it does.

nodes.label: deliver wakes the peer and enqueues rather than switching to it
nodes.norm_label: deliver wakes the peer and enqueues rather than switching to it
nodes.rationale: A direct handoff would be faster and would mean one core writing another core's stack. The slower shape is the one that survives SMP.

nodes.label: IPC is the hard one
nodes.rationale: send, receive and reply each touch two threads and an endpoint at once, and the states they move through have to change together or a message is delivered twice, or to a thread that has since died. 801 lines, every one assuming nothing else is running.

nodes.label: Not a lock or an atomic anywhere in the kernel
nodes.norm_label: not a lock or an atomic anywhere in the kernel
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion today is one sentence - there is one core, and the kernel runs with interrupts masked - and every data structure rests on it. That is the correct design for a uniprocessor and it is why ipc.c is 801 lines instead of two thousand. It does mean SMP changes the assumption the whole kernel rests on.

nodes.label: The two-year-old SMP claim, corrected
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md claimed a per-CPU struct, TPIDR_EL1 and a per-CPU runqueue from the repository's first commit, and none of the three has ever existed. It was an intention written in the present tense that nothing ever went back to.

nodes.label: tools/run_headless.py, the machine that is not there
nodes.norm_label: tools/run_headless.py, the machine that is not there
nodes.rationale: Every runner attached a framebuffer, so the machine with no display went untested and was silently broken: init asked for a screen grant that could not be given and the refused spawn was the shell. A test suite that always provides every device only tests the machine you have, and the absent device is the configuration real hardware arrives in.

nodes.label: Framebuffer drivers: pitch and channel order
nodes.norm_label: framebuffer drivers: pitch and channel order
nodes.rationale: The pitch is almost never width x 4 because the firmware aligns it, and the Pi's channel order is usually BGRA. Two details that cost an afternoon each.

nodes.label: Hardware and bring-up
nodes.rationale: Development on QEMU virt, verification on real hardware. The rule for any future target: if you cannot get a character out over serial in the first two hours, it is not a target.

nodes.label: SMP, supported by design and off
nodes.norm_label: smp, supported by design and off
nodes.rationale: With one core the bugs are deterministic; with four you debug races over UART. Known future hot spots: the page allocator, TLB shootdown and cross-core IPC.

nodes.label: The uncached framebuffer, and the backbuffer rule
nodes.norm_label: the uncached framebuffer, and the backbuffer rule
nodes.rationale: Writing to a device-mapped framebuffer is 10-50x slower than to normal RAM. Always draw into a cached backbuffer and blit one dirty rectangle at the end, which is the case write-combining handles well.

nodes.label: Cache coherency before the blit
nodes.rationale: Inner shareable rather than a manual DC CVAC over megabytes a frame, which costs more than bus coherency and is a source of forgotten bugs. The attributes of a shared surface are decided at creation in the kernel and never touched; if a Lua cache-invalidation API is needed, something was designed wrong.

nodes.label: Pitch and format travel with the handle
nodes.norm_label: pitch and format travel with the handle
nodes.rationale: No line of Lua may compute a pixel offset; the userdata holds w, h, pitch, fmt and bytes per pixel, and address arithmetic happens only in C. App surfaces are always the canonical format, so a new target changes one file. A pitch bug is invisible from inside the process - every read agrees with every write - so its test has to live outside the guest.

nodes.label: The display size as a compile-time constant
nodes.norm_label: the display size as a compile-time constant
nodes.rationale: There is no allocator, so the pixels are a static array in a NOLOAD section. Nothing above the HAL needs telling; changing it at runtime needs a capped buffer, a protocol for every holder of a geometry copy, and virtio-gpu first so there are two implementations to design against.

nodes.label: hal_fb_flush, the entry virtio-gpu will add
nodes.norm_label: hal_fb_flush, the entry virtio-gpu will add
nodes.rationale: virtio-gpu does not fit hal_fb_init's shape - it needs an explicit flush - which is exactly why adding it is what grows the interface, with two implementations in front of it rather than one.

nodes.label: hal_fb_init
nodes.rationale: Ask the firmware for a linear framebuffer and let it choose where the pixels live - the one operation ramfb and the Pi mailbox both perform.

nodes.label: hal_irq_handle
nodes.rationale: It takes no argument on purpose: the ARM side reads the GIC's IAR here, so asking the 8259 which line is in service costs two port accesses a tick and keeps arch/x86_64/trap.c from ever learning what a PIC is.
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move

nodes.label: The hal_net frame interface
nodes.rationale: Frames and nothing above them: no addresses, no protocols, no checksums. What an IP address means is not a driver's business, and a HAL that grew one would have an opinion about the internet.

nodes.label: hal_pointer_poll
nodes.rationale: Reports in the device's own units with the range beside them, because only the window manager knows how big the screen is and only it can scale.

nodes.label: hal_ticks_missed
nodes.rationale: Returns 0 on the PC and says why: the ARM timer is one-shot so a missed deadline is a comparison the re-arm was making anyway, while the PIT free-runs and the 8259 collapses repeats into one pending bit.
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move

nodes.label: The HAL interface, minimal on purpose
nodes.norm_label: the hal interface, minimal on purpose
nodes.rationale: Do not expand it speculatively: an abstraction written against a single target is that target's shape with generic names. hal.h is the authority and the listing in the document is a summary.

nodes.label: The Mac Pro 2013, rejected
nodes.rationale: No serial output at all - the RP1 problem without the back door. x86-64 in general is a better learning target than ARM; the problem is that machine.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 5, the main target
nodes.rationale: More hostile to bare metal than the Pi 4. Traps: the pitch is not width*4, BGRA rather than RGBA, an uncached framebuffer, MMIO differing from the Pi 4's, an unverified GIC version, a changed mailbox interface, and four cores started at once.

nodes.label: Remapping the 8259 before interrupts are enabled
nodes.norm_label: remapping the 8259 before interrupts are enabled
nodes.rationale: Out of reset IRQ 0-15 arrive as vectors 8-15, which are exceptions - a timer tick would report as a double fault, an accurate description of something that never happened.
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move

nodes.label: ramfb
nodes.rationale: The guest owns the configuration, so width, height and stride written back through fw_cfg is a mode change. Designing the runtime interface against it alone would produce ramfb's shape with a general name.

nodes.label: The RP1 southbridge wall
nodes.rationale: Nearly all I/O hangs off RP1 over PCIe, so a character out of the header UART would need PCIe and an RP1 driver before printf. The way out is the 3-pin JST-SH debug connector, which goes straight to the BCM2712's UART.

nodes.label: virtio-gpu
nodes.rationale: The target that earns the HAL a flush, and where a mode set is a command to the device rather than a write to a config blob.

nodes.label: AArch64's weak memory model
nodes.rationale: Far more aggressive than x86: orderings x86 forgives fail here once every thousand boots, and it is the most expensive class of bug in the project.

nodes.label: The rule for choosing a target
nodes.norm_label: the rule for choosing a target
nodes.rationale: If you cannot get a character out over serial in the first two hours, it is not a target. Everything else can be solved with time; that cannot.
nodes.source_location: The rule for choosing a target

nodes.label: bench/baselines.json
nodes.rationale: Reference numbers with date, commit and milestone. A baseline is updated by hand, never automatically, because one that updates itself detects nothing; tolerances differ with the noise - 2% under -icount, 10% on hardware.

nodes.label: tools/run_screenshot.py, the display harness
nodes.rationale: Boots QEMU, asks its monitor for the picture being scanned out and inspects it, because some properties are structurally invisible from inside the guest: geometry, the banner, channel order, a pitch bug, real key events, and a detached program still drawing. Sampling intervals aligned to something the system does are how a test comes back green about a screen it never looked at.
nodes.source_location: The display, from outside the guest

nodes.label: tools/test_kfs.lua, the host interpreter
nodes.rationale: kfs.lua is arithmetic over blocks, so with stubs every branch runs on the host in a fraction of a second - including the journal's power-loss window, a few milliseconds that five kills would usually miss. It answers 'is the format correct' and does not replace the guest tests.

nodes.label: make browser, a camera with checks on it
nodes.norm_label: make browser, a camera with checks on it
nodes.rationale: make web answers over serial because each of its results is a number the guest can say; the browser cannot be, so a page is served from the host, the screen is looked at, and the picture is written whether it passes or fails. The checks are deliberately blunt because a check that goes stale is worse than none, and what the page says is deliberately not compared against a reference.

nodes.label: C self-tests
nodes.rationale: Before Lua exists there is no other option. The special case that must be anticipated when the vector is written: several tests verify that something fails correctly, which needs a handler that records an expected exception and continues.

nodes.label: The scores are a geometric mean
nodes.norm_label: the scores are a geometric mean
nodes.rationale: Because they are ratios: the arithmetic mean of twice as fast at one thing and half as fast at another is 1.25, which claims the machine is better when it is exactly even.

nodes.label: The harness: runner on the host, tests in the guest, serial the channel
nodes.norm_label: the harness: runner on the host, tests in the guest, serial the channel
nodes.rationale: make test and make bench use separate images and runners because -icount makes QEMU several times slower and the tests must not pay for it. Build it at M0 with the first line of output; a harness that is deferred never gets built.

nodes.label: Host-driven integration tests
nodes.rationale: Scenarios needing several processes and coordination, where the system's properties get tested rather than its functions.

nodes.label: -icount determinism
nodes.rationale: The same spin loop measures 88187, 88687 and 89062 across ordinary runs and 75001, 75000, 75001 under -icount; with interrupts masked the numbers are bit-identical, which is why a 2% tolerance is generous.

nodes.label: Lua tests, run at EL0 in a process
nodes.norm_label: lua tests, run at el0 in a process
nodes.rationale: From M5 the kernel has no interpreter, so the plan and the names stay on the C side and the assertions live out in user/tests/luatest.lua. A failing assertion errors and init prints it; that line is not TAP, so the runner ignores it and a human gets the reason.

nodes.label: Tests as milestone gates
nodes.rationale: Each milestone's definition of done becomes a test that is never deleted, so the full suite is the history of the project and a break in M3's IPC surfaces on the commit rather than three weeks later.

nodes.label: make powertest
nodes.rationale: SIGKILL five times at five instants during four hundred writes, then boot and ask whether every name reads and every file holds what was written. A missing file is fine; a half-written one, or a name pointing at an inode never written, is not.

nodes.label: score and sysbench
nodes.rationale: make bench answers 'did this change make it slower' on this desk; score answers 'is this board faster than that board'. Fixed time rather than fixed work, batch size found rather than chosen, units declared rather than inferred from a return value, and a batch size that changes what a unit costs is a broken measurement.

nodes.label: Semihosting for the guest's exit code
nodes.norm_label: semihosting for the guest's exit code
nodes.rationale: HLT #0xF000 with SYS_EXIT terminates QEMU with the guest's code, and gives a watchdog a way to abort a hung test. Without it the host kills QEMU on a timeout and guesses.

nodes.label: The TAP protocol over the UART
nodes.norm_label: the tap protocol over the uart
nodes.rationale: The guest prints a plan and ok/not ok lines; a forty-line host script launches QEMU, parses the serial and exits with the matching code.

nodes.label: The arrow keys are not broken
nodes.norm_label: the arrow keys are not broken
nodes.rationale: Written down so it is not chased a third time: every stage of the input path is correct and what fails is the harness, at a different phase each run, correlating with load on the host. A control that shares the variable it controls for is not a control, and a probe must be checked against an input known to arrive.

nodes.label: The blind spot a benchmark suite has by construction
nodes.norm_label: the blind spot a benchmark suite has by construction
nodes.rationale: bench/ measures operations and cannot measure the system they run in. The idle thread cost a full timer period per yield - the whole system roughly a thousand times slower - with every number in bench/ green. Two lessons: latency between operations needs its own measurement, and where a test can run decides what it can see. Measure the floor before believing a slope.

nodes.label: A check that survives deleting its rule is not testing that rule
nodes.norm_label: a check that survives deleting its rule is not testing that rule
nodes.rationale: Every check was deleted in turn to confirm it fails without its rule. The 'was it committed' test did not fail: the uncommitted case blanked the journal header, so recovery refused it for having no magic and the state field was never exercised. It took three attempts and each wrong one passed.

nodes.label: QEMU and hardware measure different things
nodes.norm_label: qemu and hardware measure different things
nodes.rationale: QEMU is a JIT translator, so wall time in it means nothing - but with -icount it is deterministic, which makes it the right instrument for detecting regressions. Hardware has the truth via PMCCNTR_EL0, and under QEMU the PMU is not faithfully emulated.

nodes.label: Correctness, budget, regression
nodes.rationale: Three different things that get conflated: does it do what it says, does it fit the time it has, and did it get worse since yesterday. Each needs its own mechanism, and a single performance number answers none of them.

nodes.label: What to resist when measuring
nodes.rationale: Do not measure everything, do not optimise against QEMU, do not chase a number that is inside budget, and do not delete an old test because we know that works by now - that is exactly the test that catches the regression.

nodes.label: C discipline and the mandatory flags
nodes.norm_label: c discipline and the mandatory flags
nodes.rationale: -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fno-common -fno-strict-aliasing, plus mmio_read32/mmio_write32 with the barriers inside, stack guard pages, UBSan with an own handler, and _Static_assert on every struct crossing into assembly.

nodes.label: The x86-64 context switch
nodes.rationale: Seventy-two bytes against AArch64's 656, and the difference is System V rather than the processor: every XMM register is caller-saved, so a thread that called the switch has already spilled its floating point. One stack moves rather than two, and rip cannot be moved to, so the restore pushes it and returns.

nodes.label: CR0.WP, without which a read-only mapping is decoration
nodes.norm_label: cr0.wp, without which a read-only mapping is decoration
nodes.rationale: Out of reset a ring 0 write to a page with RW clear succeeds; the permission is enforced against ring 3 only, and AArch64 has no counterpart. Found by narrowing .text, reading the entry back correct, and watching a deliberate store go through.

nodes.label: CR4.SMEP, and why SMAP is off
nodes.norm_label: cr4.smep, and why smap is off
nodes.rationale: One NX bit covers both privilege levels where ARM has PXN and UXN, so SMEP buys the guarantee with a control register instead of a descriptor bit. SMAP is deliberately off because the kernel reads user memory on every IPC.

nodes.label: The GDT, the TSS and ring 3
nodes.norm_label: the gdt, the tss and ring 3
nodes.rationale: A privilege level on ARM is bits in PSTATE; here it is a property of a segment descriptor. The order is arithmetic rather than convention because syscall and sysretq derive CS and SS from IA32_STAR. gdt_init runs before mmu_init because the processor writes the accessed bit into a descriptor.

nodes.label: The GIC version is not the default
nodes.norm_label: the gic version is not the default
nodes.rationale: -M virt gives a GICv2; Kosmos drives a GICv3, so gic-version=3 is on the QEMU line, and booting on a plain -M virt finds no redistributor and never receives an interrupt. The fastest way to settle it is to dump the device tree rather than to remember.

nodes.label: NVIDIA Jetson, a cheap port
nodes.rationale: Same ISA, so only hal/ changes and it is a week. Against it: NVIDIA's signed boot chain makes the iteration cycle much worse than copying a file to an SD card.

nodes.label: make KVM=1 x86
nodes.rationale: Runs on an x86-64 Linux host's own cores and needs -cpu host, the same trade make fast makes on ARM; it does nothing on an Apple Silicon Mac.

nodes.label: Lazy FP save, on either machine
nodes.norm_label: lazy fp save, on either machine
nodes.rationale: -mno-mmx -mno-sse -mno-sse2 are this architecture's -mgeneral-regs-only: the kernel may not touch a floating-point register at all, and a flag turns that from a promise into a compile error, so a kernel thread never faults because it never can. CR0.TS is the disarm and vector 7 the fault.

nodes.label: Building long mode
nodes.rationale: ARM hands you 64-bit execution and asks which privilege level; x86 starts in real mode and long mode has to be built - page tables, a GDT with the L bit, CR4.PAE, EFER.LME, CR0.PG and a far jump, in that order. Page tables live in .bss so zeroing must come first; rdmsr answers in EDX:EAX; a multiboot loader parses ELF32, so the a.out kludge bit is what makes an ELF64 image loadable.

nodes.label: -mno-red-zone
nodes.rationale: The red zone is 128 bytes below rsp a leaf function may use without adjusting the stack pointer, and an interrupt handler pushes straight over it. Nothing notices until there are interrupts, which is the worst time to find out.

nodes.label: x86-64 paging: four levels and accumulating permissions
nodes.norm_label: x86-64 paging: four levels and accumulating permissions
nodes.rationale: The bottom three levels are ARM's L1/L2/L3 exactly and everything lives under 512 GB, so the extra level costs one page. Permissions accumulate down the walk, so intermediate entries are permissive and the leaf carries the policy - any other arrangement stores one permission in four places that can disagree.

nodes.label: PowerPC G4, the port that teaches the most
nodes.norm_label: powerpc g4, the port that teaches the most
nodes.rationale: Valuable because it is big-endian, which lands in one precise place - the Lua table serializer - and forces an explicit wire format. Open Firmware solves the console; the cost is an inverted hashed page table with no analogy to a radix tree.

nodes.label: QEMU virt aarch64, the development target
nodes.norm_label: qemu virt aarch64, the development target
nodes.rationale: PL011, GIC and virtio: standard, documented, serial straight to the terminal. Which exception level you get depends on the options, so read CurrentEL rather than assuming; secondary cores start and must be parked.

nodes.label: The recommended porting order
nodes.rationale: QEMU virt, Pi 1, Pi 5, Jetson, G4 - easiest to debug first. Each jump breaks a different assumption, and porting before the design is proven generalises over assumptions not yet known to be correct.

nodes.label: syscall does not switch the stack
nodes.norm_label: syscall does not switch the stack
nodes.rationale: For two instructions the kernel runs at ring 0 on a stack the process chose, which is why IA32_FMASK clears IF. The kernel stack comes out of the TSS, so there is one answer to which stack an entry lands on rather than two that can disagree.

nodes.label: virtio.c, below the HAL
nodes.rationale: Four devices speak virtio-mmio and the handshake is identical while the rings are not, so the conversation is shared and the ring is not. It is not a HAL interface - no other board implements it - which is why it lives under the board.

nodes.label: Two devices that are the same device
nodes.norm_label: two devices that are the same device
nodes.rationale: Keyboard and tablet are both virtio-input, device id 18, indistinguishable in the register window; telling them apart means asking each what events it can produce, which costs a partial bring-up. The file is instance-based because two devices of a kind cannot share a ring.
nodes.source_location: Two devices that are the same device

nodes.label: x86-64, the second architecture
nodes.rationale: It runs the desktop on QEMU q35 and passes the same 62 display checks in the same time as aarch64. Cost, once kernel/ compiled, was almost entirely device plumbing; with two AArch64 targets the layer boundary is a promise, and with x86-64 it becomes a compile error.
nodes.source_location: x86-64, and what a second architecture cost

nodes.label: arch/ versus hal/
nodes.rationale: arch/ is 'which CPU are you' and is reimplemented rather than abstracted; hal/ is 'which peripheral do you have' and does get a common interface, because pushing out a character is pushing out a character. Two boards with the same CPU share arch/ and differ in hal/.

nodes.label: Endianness, which turned out to be free
nodes.norm_label: endianness, which turned out to be free
nodes.rationale: Checked rather than assumed: every string.pack in the on-disk format carries an explicit <, the network stack's put16/get16 do explicit shifts, and IPC structs never cross architectures because both ends are processes on the same machine.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 1, the argument answered no
nodes.norm_label: raspberry pi 1, the argument answered no
nodes.rationale: Kept rather than deleted because it was a good argument: GPIO 14/15 are UART directly, one core, canonical mailbox framebuffer, and ARMv6 would force arch/ and hal/ genuinely apart. Refused because it is 32-bit - a complete second arch/armv6/ on a 700 MHz core, for a system whose question is whether it can be fast - and because x86-64 surfaces the same assumptions from a better direction.

nodes.label: Capability
nodes.rationale: A permission that is also the only way to name something. If you were not handed the capability, you cannot even name the resource.

nodes.label: RP1 - the Pi 5 southbridge
nodes.rationale: USB, Ethernet and the header GPIO hang off it over PCIe. It is what makes the Pi 5 hostile to bare metal.

nodes.label: Capabilities, from seL4
nodes.rationale: An index into your own table, never a global identifier. What you were not given, you cannot name.
nodes.source_location: And the rest of what it is built out of

nodes.label: Real hardware, a Raspberry Pi 5
nodes.rationale: Chosen because it is hard: a desktop that feels fast on it is a result rather than an emulator number. Every performance question is currently answered 'measure it on the Pi', and the Pi is not here yet.

nodes.label: The ARM GNU bare-metal toolchain
nodes.rationale: aarch64-none-elf, downloaded from ARM's site: genuinely bare metal with no Linux assumptions, shipping gcc, binutils and gdb in one tarball with nothing to build.

nodes.label: 3-pin JST-SH debug UART cable, pending
nodes.rationale: It blocks the Pi 5 target. Until then, all work happens under QEMU.

nodes.label: ARM Architecture Reference Manual (ARMv8-A)
nodes.rationale: The source of truth for exceptions, page tables and barriers.

nodes.label: eLua
nodes.rationale: Prior art for Lua on bare metal.

nodes.label: seL4
nodes.rationale: For thinking about IPC and capability design.

nodes.label: The default in an instruction should be the machine it was written on
nodes.norm_label: the default in an instruction should be the machine it was written on
nodes.rationale: The commands used to say darwin-x86_64 with a note to swap it. Following them exactly gave a tarball that does not run; following them nearly exactly gave 'aarch64-none-elf-gcc: No such file or directory', which says the compiler is missing rather than that the path has the wrong architecture in it. An hour of a session went into that.

nodes.label: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine is not optional
nodes.rationale: macOS quarantines anything downloaded through a browser or curl, and without clearing it Gatekeeper kills the binaries with a message that does not say why.

nodes.label: The kernel needs a compiler; the userland needs a compiler and a libm
nodes.norm_label: the kernel needs a compiler; the userland needs a compiler and a libm
nodes.rationale: Homebrew's aarch64-elf-gcc compiles the whole tree cleanly and cannot link the user image, because it ships no C library. The userland depends on the toolchain's libm for thirteen functions - pow, exp, log, log2, log10, sqrt, fmod, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan2 - which newlib supplies from ARM's tarball. runtime/libc/math.c supplies only the six that are exact bit manipulation. Writing the missing thirteen by hand is not a tidy-up: a plausible wrong answer in a font rasteriser looks like a rendering bug rather than an arithmetic one. This is the shape of the question the Pi will ask, and it is not a HAL question.

nodes.label: Do not use aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
nodes.rationale: It brings glibc, Linux start files and a dynamic loader, which is exactly what -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostartfiles exists to avoid.

nodes.label: Capabilities are already nearly safe
nodes.rationale: They live in struct thread as caps[CAPS_PER_THREAD], so a thread's table is touched by that thread and nobody else - except when one is granted, which is the one path that needs care. Luck worth naming.

nodes.label: Kosmos
nodes.rationale: A microkernel desktop OS with a Lua userland, built to learn and to test ideas that exist but rarely appear together; it competes with nothing, which is what allows decisions a commercial OS cannot take.

nodes.label: The UI kit and its consistency rule
nodes.norm_label: the ui kit and its consistency rule
nodes.rationale: An app does not draw UI primitives: the kit lives in /lib/ui and is resolved by namespace, with visual tokens in /system/ui/theme. Editing button.lua changes every app the next time one starts.

nodes.label: The app server and window manager
nodes.norm_label: the app server and window manager
nodes.rationale: Windows, decoration, stacking, focus, workspaces, compositing and input routing, all in Lua except the blit. It knows nothing about views.

nodes.label: The UI build order
nodes.rationale: Windows, view tree, follow modes, basic widgets done at M6; workspaces, stack and tile, replicants and shared-memory surfaces at M7.

nodes.label: Control-W, the one reserved key
nodes.rationale: The first version took Tab and the arrows, which decides no application may have a second control. With no modifiers to escape into, it takes screen and tmux's approach: one key that introduces a command rather than being one.

nodes.label: Window decoration and the full-width frame
nodes.norm_label: window decoration and the full-width frame
nodes.rationale: BeOS made a tab only as wide as its title so stacked windows kept their titles readable; Kosmos does not stack windows, so it bought nothing, and the bar now spans the window with the border taking its colour.

nodes.label: Follow modes, and no constraint solver
nodes.norm_label: follow modes, and no constraint solver
nodes.rationale: A solver is thousands of lines with non-obvious behaviour when overdetermined; follow modes are fifty lines and cover 90%. The document described the list form while ui.lua read the set form, and nothing caught it because no application had ever used follow - the entire layout path was dead code that happened to compile.

nodes.label: The UI kit (lib/ui.lua)
nodes.rationale: A library running inside the app's process: view tree, layout, event routing and the generation of drawing commands. If it has a bug the app dies and nothing else.

nodes.label: Messages as tables with a type field
nodes.norm_label: messages as tables with a type field
nodes.rationale: A BMessage was a typed dictionary with a four-byte what; here it is a Lua table with a type, which is the same concept without the marshalling. An input event, a message to the app server and a filesystem read are the same class of thing.

nodes.label: A press grabs
nodes.rationale: Everything until the release goes to the window and view the press landed in, even after the pointer has left; without it, releasing outside leaves two controls half-operated. A press on a title bar is the manager's, anywhere else is the application's.

nodes.label: Stack and tile
nodes.rationale: Haiku's two additions worth having from the start: several windows sharing one frame with tabs side by side, and attached windows that resize together. They come almost free out of the tab model.

nodes.label: Themes, and colours named rather than captured
nodes.norm_label: themes, and colours named rather than captured
nodes.rationale: The palette table is mutated in place, never replaced, so every widget reading theme.text at draw time follows the change with nothing subscribing. A colour may be a number or a palette name resolved on every draw; capturing theme.text_dim at construction freezes it, which left a light theme with near-invisible headings.

nodes.label: The view tree
nodes.rationale: A view is a rectangle in its parent's coordinates, as BView was. Nested coordinates, automatic clipping, bottom-up hit testing, and invalidation by region - damage tracking falls out of the tree rather than out of a heuristic.

nodes.label: Workspaces
nodes.rationale: BeOS had 32 with independent resolution each; here they are one more field in the window struct and a filter in the compositor.

nodes.label: The seven principles
nodes.rationale: Non-negotiable decisions; if a feature collides with one, the feature is cut. The 10k-line kernel figure is a symptom of 'the kernel does not know what a file is', not a rule of its own.

nodes.label: A Lua table until a declared struct
nodes.norm_label: a lua table until a declared struct
nodes.rationale: The language's data model where the shape is the caller's to choose, a declared struct where the shape is agreed. A server must stay correct when its caller is wrong, and a collector cannot sit where something else's timing depends on it. Cost: editing a header rebuilds both sides, errors become numbers, hot reload gone.

nodes.label: The dimensional look
nodes.rationale: Reversed September 2026: committing to dimensionality is a design language, not a costume - raised means press this, sunken means content lives here, a groove means these are separate. Every desktop converges on the same flat rectangle, and Kosmos owes compatibility to nothing. The surviving rule: copy behaviour that was got right, decide shading fresh.

nodes.label: Hover is not sent
nodes.rationale: Every movement would be a message and the path would run at the rate the pointer moves rather than at the rate anything changes. Movement is sent while a button is held, because that is what a control needs to un-press when you slide off it.

nodes.label: 0.8 - a web browser, and a network under it
nodes.norm_label: 0.8 - a web browser, and a network under it
nodes.rationale: NetSurf's hubbub, libdom and libcss vendored unpatched on a freestanding libc. TCP so a page can come off the real internet, and an HTTP server to go the other way. The allocator learned to grow. And the 64-bit-only line was drawn deliberately, which is what ruled the Pi 1 out.

nodes.label: What there is to try
nodes.rationale: wm browser, wm tracker, wm terminal, wm cube3d, wm doom, wm paint, ping 8.8.8.8, wm webserver.

nodes.label: A box model
nodes.rationale: Margins, padding, borders, width, floats. Images and forms both wait on it.

nodes.label: Forms
nodes.rationale: They need a box that takes keys.

nodes.label: Images in the browser
nodes.rationale: stb_image is already vendored for the PDF reader.

nodes.label: Networking, built
nodes.rationale: virtio-net, ARP, IP, ICMP and TCP with shared rings, an HTTP server, a telnet client. It reaches the real internet through QEMU's NAT.

nodes.label: A resolver
nodes.rationale: An address is four numbers today, which is the single biggest thing between the browser and the web. UDP exists in the stack only as much as DNS needs - no sockets, because nothing else has asked for any.

nodes.label: A web browser
nodes.rationale: hubbub, libdom and libcss running at EL0: HTML parsed into a DOM, the CSS cascade run with a user-agent stylesheet, text laid out into boxes that survive the paint, and links you can click.

nodes.label: Back button and link are two ways to the same place
nodes.norm_label: back button and link are two ways to the same place
nodes.rationale: The return link is also a link, so both paths have to work.

nodes.label: No box model
nodes.rationale: Blocks are stacked and inline content flows; everything else about geometry is a constant in a header.

nodes.label: The cascade parses and nothing asks it
nodes.norm_label: the cascade parses and nothing asks it
nodes.rationale: libcss parses, selects and answers, and nothing asks it. Colour, font size, weight and slant should come from the computed style rather than from the tag's name.

nodes.label: Forms - a box that takes keys
nodes.norm_label: forms - a box that takes keys
nodes.rationale: It needs boxes to be addressable from outside the layout - the same step that made the link clickable.

nodes.label: Images - plumbing rather than a decoder
nodes.norm_label: images - plumbing rather than a decoder
nodes.rationale: stb_image is already vendored for the PDF reader.

nodes.label: link_at
nodes.rationale: Finds the laid-out run under a clicked point.

nodes.label: List indent and hanging indent
nodes.rationale: Twenty-four pixels with a marker; the second line of a long item lines up under the first rather than under the margin. The marker is a disc for every item, which is wrong for an ol - list-style comes from the cascade, and the cascade is not consulted here yet.

nodes.label: No box model and no colour from the cascade
nodes.norm_label: no box model and no colour from the cascade
nodes.rationale: The stylesheet at the top of the file parses and nothing on the page is drawn from it; faces are chosen by tag. The page says so rather than pretending otherwise.

nodes.label: Layout keeps its runs
nodes.rationale: A word is where a font change, a link's hit rectangle and a selection all attach. That is why layout keeps its runs.

nodes.label: Six things that have to work to arrive here
nodes.norm_label: six things that have to work to arrive here
nodes.rationale: The layout kept its boxes, the click was turned into a point on the page, link_at found the run under it, the relative address was resolved against the one the browser was on, and the whole fetch happened again. The only way to know all six work is to arrive here.

nodes.label: Lua coroutines as the concurrency model
nodes.norm_label: lua coroutines as the concurrency model
nodes.rationale: Concurrency inside a process with zero synchronisation; one server serves many clients on one stack and each conversation is written straight through with a yield where it would have waited. There are no kernel threads and no syscall to make one.

nodes.label: diskfs and kfs.lua
nodes.rationale: The one server left in Lua, and not for the usual reasons: its core runs on the host as well as the guest, which is what lets make test check the journal's power-loss window without booting a machine.

nodes.label: Hot reload, removed September 2026
nodes.rationale: First demoted below responsiveness, then made moot: seven servers moved to C and there is no dynamic linking, so none can be reloaded. What survives is the shape - serve still takes a factory, so state and behaviour stay separate.

nodes.label: The journal checksum measurement
nodes.rationale: Files a second: 21.0 before the journal, 14.4 with an FNV-1a checksum in Lua, 20.5 with it stubbed out, 16.7 with it in C. The journal's own structure cost about 2%; hashing four kilobytes a byte at a time cost the other thirty.

nodes.label: kfs.store as the measurement that would settle it
nodes.norm_label: kfs.store as the measurement that would settle it
nodes.rationale: Self-contained, already measured, and testable on the host, so a C version can be held to the same checks. Prediction on record: fifteen percent, because a file create is block I/O and round trips that no language changes.

nodes.label: Vanilla Lua 5.4
nodes.rationale: 30k lines of readable C89, designed to be embedded in a hostile environment, first-class coroutines, and tables as the only structured type so the protocol can be the data model. LuaJIT stays out: stuck on 5.1 and hostile on bare-metal AArch64.

nodes.label: NET_OP_POLL and its two readiness masks
nodes.norm_label: net_op_poll and its two readiness masks
nodes.rationale: Ready is not a single question: a reader wants to hear that bytes arrived, a writer that room appeared. The version that guessed with one mask deadlocked.

nodes.label: Share-nothing userland, one lua_State per process
nodes.norm_label: share-nothing userland, one lua_state per process
nodes.rationale: Concurrency complexity stays confined to the kernel.

nodes.label: The split: the kit in the app, the server apart
nodes.norm_label: the split: the kit in the app, the server apart
nodes.rationale: UI complexity lives in the app, where it can crash without consequence; to the server a window is a rectangle with an endpoint on the other side. That boundary is the one BeOS had and it is correct.

nodes.label: Known risks
nodes.rationale: No types over tens of thousands of lines of Lua, no libraries, no visual debugger, a stage that can stall for months, and the temptation to push things down to C because it is faster.

nodes.label: The C/Lua language split
nodes.rationale: C is what touches hardware or defines the isolation boundary; Lua is everything else. If a bug can corrupt another process it goes in C; if it can only kill its own process it goes in Lua. Almost none of the C is in the kernel - the interpreter, gfx.c and stb_truetype run at EL0.

nodes.label: No LuaRocks
nodes.rationale: Structural incompatibility rather than dogma: no dlopen, no ELF loader, no full libc, and LuaRocks is itself a Unix app. Deeper: io.open('/etc/passwd') is semantically incoherent here, so importing such libraries is POSIX through the back door.

nodes.label: Structure in Lua, loops over bytes in C
nodes.norm_label: structure in lua, loops over bytes in c
nodes.rationale: Decisions, dispatch, protocol, state and layout are measurably cheap in Lua; loops over many bytes, pixels or samples are measurably expensive. Only a profile can say which.

nodes.label: Why C and not Rust
nodes.rationale: Lua is 30k lines of C at the system's centre, so a Rust kernel gets Rust's costs with no guarantee where the risk is. And Lua's error handling uses longjmp, which skips every Drop on the hot path.

nodes.label: No locks: coroutines instead of BLoopers
nodes.norm_label: no locks: coroutines instead of bloopers
nodes.rationale: In BeOS every BWindow was a thread and forgetting Lock() was the number one source of app bugs; the whole locking API existed because threads shared memory. Here each window is a coroutine, so the class of bug does not exist, and a busy window still does not freeze the others because each yields at its receive.

nodes.label: What is not copied from BeOS
nodes.norm_label: what is not copied from beos
nodes.rationale: The C++ class hierarchy, BLooper as a system thread, the entire locking API, the four-byte what codes, and the Translation Kit. The hierarchy existed because 1990s C++ had no better way to express composition.

nodes.label: GIC
nodes.rationale: GICv2 and GICv3 are quite different from each other; the Pi 5 and QEMU virt use v3.

nodes.label: TPIDR_EL1
nodes.rationale: A register reserved by convention to point at the per-CPU struct. The glossary claims using it from day one makes SMP cheap later; smp.md records that it has never been written.

nodes.label: get-and-run-kosmos.sh - one command to run it
nodes.norm_label: get-and-run-kosmos.sh - one command to run it
nodes.rationale: Nothing to clone, nothing to build, no toolchain. It fetches the newest published image, the runner and a disk; QEMU is the only thing it cannot fetch. The framebuffer size is compiled in, so a different resolution is a different image.

nodes.label: 0.9 - a second architecture
nodes.rationale: x86-64 as well as AArch64, running the whole desktop. All thirteen kernel/ files compile for both with no #ifdef, and the display harness passes the same sixty-two checks on each board in the same time.

nodes.label: hal/virtio - shared drivers, per-board transport
nodes.rationale: The four virtio drivers moved into a shared directory rather than being rewritten, with each board bringing its own transport: fixed offsets from a device-tree window on one, a walk of the PCI capability list on the other. Same sequence, every register somewhere else.

nodes.label: SMP, and real parallelism
nodes.rationale: The x86-64 port paid part of it forward: two pieces of state are per-CPU rather than per-thread - the TSS and whoever owns the floating-point registers - and finding the boundary was not theoretical. A global holding the interrupted stack pointer looked like per-CPU state, was per-thread, and produced a process returning to user level on another process's stack.

nodes.label: x86-64, under QEMU - done
nodes.rationale: All thirteen kernel/*.c compile for it with no #ifdef, and the whole userland - fifty thousand lines - needed about a hundred and ten lines of assembly and one #if. The 64-bit line was drawn where it was precisely so this would not be a refactor.

nodes.label: x86-64 SMP is a new driver: local APIC and ACPI MADT
nodes.norm_label: x86-64 smp is a new driver: local apic and acpi madt
nodes.rationale: Kosmos drives the 8259 PIC. SMP needs the local APIC for IPIs and a per-core timer, because one 8253 cannot tick four cores, plus ACPI MADT parsing to find the cores and their APIC ids. That is a table walker and an interrupt controller, neither of which exists - most of the reason the two boards are not equal work. Then INIT-SIPI-SIPI and a real-mode trampoline page under 1 MB.

nodes.label: The register that finds the per-CPU struct
nodes.norm_label: the register that finds the per-cpu struct
